steps.say: Tiny premature babies lose much more water through their skin and breathing than full term babies do. An open warmer, blue light treatment and breathing difficulty all drive that unseen loss even higher.
steps.tx: A premature baby loses more water through skin and breathing than a term baby. **Insensible water loss** (unseen skin and lung water loss) runs **45 to 60 mL per kg per day** (forty five to sixty millilitres per kilogram per day) in babies under **1500 g** (one thousand five hundred grams), but only **30 to 35 mL per kg per day** (thirty to thirty five millilitres per kilogram per day) at term. A **radiant warmer** (open heated bed), **phototherapy** (blue light treatment) and respiratory distress each push losses higher.

rows: 45 to 60 mL per kg per day
30 to 35 mL per kg per day

steps.say: A newborn is expected to lose up to a tenth of birth weight in the first few days as extra water leaves the body. By day four the daily maintenance fluid reaches about a hundred to a hundred thirty mls per kilo, and gut catastrophes demand far more.
steps.tx: Every newborn shrinks a little as extra body water leaves after birth. **Physiologic water loss** (normal early weight drop) reaches **10 percent** (ten percent) of body weight over the first **3 to 5 days** (three to five days) of life. By day **4** (four) the **maintenance fluids** (daily drip volume) reach **100 to 130 mL per kg per day** (one hundred to one hundred thirty millilitres per kilogram per day). Babies with **gastroschisis** (open abdominal wall defect) or **necrotising enterocolitis** (dying gut emergency) need much more.

vis.alt: Reference chart with dehydration grading table by four clinical signs, ORS composition and Plans A, B and C illustrations.
vis.caption: Dehydration grading with ORS Plans A, B and C. Neonatal maintenance fluids reach 100 to 130 mL per kg per day by day 4. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Watch the nappy output to judge whether your fluids are keeping up. A newborn should pass at least one to two mls per kilo every hour, and a young kidney concentrates weakly, so falling output warns early.
steps.tx: Urine output is the bedside gauge of whether fluids are enough. The minimum acceptable **urine output** (wee volume) in a newborn is **1 to 2 mL per kg per hour** (one to two millilitres per kilogram per hour). When kidneys are dry but healthy, in **prerenal azotemia** (dry kidney strain), the **urine osmolarity** (urine concentration) reaches only about **700 mOsm per kg** (seven hundred milliosmoles per kilogram), far below adult power, so small shortfalls show fast.

rows: Output 1 to 2 mL per kg per hour

steps.say: After the first couple of days babies need salt and potassium added to their drip, not just sugar water. The standard bag is five percent dextrose in half strength saline with twenty units of potassium per litre.
steps.tx: Salt and potassium must be added once the early water loss phase passes. Daily **sodium requirement** (salt need) is **2 to 4 mEq per kg** (two to four milliequivalents per kilogram) and **potassium requirement** (potassium need) is **1 to 2 mEq per kg** (one to two milliequivalents per kilogram). The usual fluid is **5 percent dextrose** (sugar water) in **0.45 percent saline** (half strength salt water) with **20 mEq per L** (twenty milliequivalents per litre) of potassium, run as the **maintenance fluids** (daily drip) rate.

vis.alt: Diagram of ADH action in the collecting duct with a comparison of SIADH versus hypovolaemic hyponatraemia causes, urine findings and treatment.
vis.caption: Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from gut loss is replaced with isotonic saline, while SIADH needs fluid restriction. Daily neonatal sodium need is 2 to 4 mEq per kg. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Replace what the baby actually loses, matching the fluid to the source. Stomach aspirate is topped up with half strength saline with potassium, while watery stool, stoma drainage or bile needs balanced Ringer fluid instead.
steps.tx: Vomit and fistula losses are replaced drop for drop with matching fluid. **Gastric losses** (vomit and tube aspirate) are replaced volume for volume with **0.45 percent saline** (half strength salt water) carrying **20 mEq per L** (twenty milliequivalents per litre) of potassium. **Diarrhoeal** (watery stool), pancreatic and **biliary losses** (liver bile drainage) plus **ostomy output** (stoma drainage) are isotonic, so they are replaced with **lactated Ringer** (balanced salt fluid), not with weak saline.

steps.say: A baby who has bled needs blood products quickly, not just salty water. Give ten to twenty mls per kilo of packed red cells, plasma or albumin as a bolus, then reassess and hunt the source.
steps.tx: **Hypovolemia** (empty circulation) from acute **hemorrhage** (sudden blood loss) is corrected promptly with blood products given as a **fluid bolus** (fast volume push) of **10 to 20 mL per kg** (ten to twenty millilitres per kilogram) of **packed red blood cells** (concentrated red cells), plasma or **5 percent albumin** (five percent protein fluid). Reassess after each bolus and look for the bleeding source while volume goes in, since fluids alone cannot carry oxygen.

steps.say: Infection in a newborn shows only as small behaviour changes, so keep suspicion high. Poor feeds, wobbly temperature, slow refill, fast breathing or extra irritability should trigger blood, urine and spinal fluid cultures first.
steps.tx: Newborn infection hides behind tiny behaviour changes. **Sepsis workup** (infection hunt) covers **blood** (bloodstream culture), urine and **cerebrospinal fluid** (spine fluid) cultures. Subtle triggers include **feeding intolerance** (vomits and big aspirates), temperature instability, poor refill, **tachypnea** (fast breathing) and irritability. Any one of these in a surgical baby should prompt cultures before antibiotics start, since missed infection kills faster than most surgical disease.

steps.say: The first antibiotics must hit the three classic nursery killers, which are group B strep, resistant staph and E coli. Each drip, drain and breathing tube raises hospital infection risk, so review every line every day.
steps.tx: First antibiotics must cover the killers of the nursery. Empiric cover targets **group B streptococcus** (birth canal germ), **methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus** (drug resistant skin germ) and **Escherichia coli** (gut germ). Invasive **lines and tubes** (drips, drains and breathing tubes) raise hospital acquired infection risk, so every extra device day adds danger and every line needs a daily reason to stay in place.
